intro: A ductless system has no ducts. It pushes refrigerant through a small line set to an indoor head that blows air into one room or one zone, and a matching outdoor unit that dumps the heat somewhere else entirely, so installing one is largely a question of where the outdoor unit can physically live and how the lines reach the head. The company that covers your area looks at the property and tells you what is feasible before anything gets mounted.
whatHappens: Survey the property for an outdoor spot with airflow, shade, and a place for the line set
Confirm the capacity against the load of the room rather than the square footage of the house
Route the line set through a small wall penetration, insulated and sealed
Mount the indoor head high enough that the air reaches the whole room
Run the condensate line to a drain and prove the system holds pressure
howPriced: The cost is driven by how many heads, how far the line set travels, and what has to be drilled or opened to get there. One head through an exterior wall is the simple version, while multiple zones or a head on the far side of the house means longer runs, more line set, and possibly a new sleeve or a wall patch. Time of day matters less than location on a job like this, and a unit in direct sun or squeezed into a tight corner works harder and wears out sooner, so the technician may recommend a different spot than the one you picked.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to install a ductless mini split?
faqs.a: It depends on the number of heads and how far the line set has to run. A single head on an outside wall is the least involved job. Multiple zones, longer runs, or drilling through brick or finished walls all add labor. The company that covers your area will quote after seeing the property.

faqs.q: Do I need central air if I am getting a mini split?
faqs.a: Often not. A ductless head can handle an addition, a garage, a shop, or a second floor that never got its own ductwork. If the rest of the house already has a central system, the mini split often serves as a supplement rather than a replacement.

faqs.q: Where do you put the outdoor unit for a ductless system?
faqs.a: Somewhere with moving air around it, out of direct afternoon sun, and far enough from fences, shrubs, and walls to pull a proper volume. It also needs to sit level and drain away from the foundation. Placement can cost more than the equipment itself if the clearances are tight.

faqs.q: How many mini splits do I need for my house?
faqs.a: One head per zone you want conditioned, sized for the load of that zone. A load calculation on each room is the only honest way to pick capacity. Oversizing a head gives you short cycling and a unit that never dehumidifies properly.

faqs.q: Can a ductless system cool more than one room?
faqs.a: Yes, with multiple heads fed by one outdoor unit. That is a multi zone setup, and it costs more than a single head because of the additional line sets and controls. Each head can also be run on its own schedule.

faqs.q: Does a mini split installation need a permit?
faqs.a: In most places, yes, because the line set is a refrigerant line and the electrical feed has to be permitted. The contractor handles the paperwork as part of the installation. Ask to see the permit record after the work is finished.
